newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Racism "most divisive issue" for Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Racism "most divisive issue" for Australia.

text.p: Racism is the most divisive human rights issue facing Australia, the president of Australia's Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission said on Tuesday.
Sir Ron Wilson said 1996 had not been a very good year for human rights in Australia, with virulent racism surfacing towards Asians and Aborigines.

"Racism is the single most potentially divise human rights issue confronting Australians today -- a threat to social cohesion and to the ties that have bound us until now," Wilson said in his annual speech on International Human Rights Day.
"In the past year virulent expressions of racism towards Asian people have merged with an appalling level of denigration of indigenous Australians," said Wilson.

Wilson criticised the race debate which has engulfed Australia since September when independent politician Pauline Hanson charged that Asians were swamping Australia and disadvantaged Aborigines were given preferential treatment.
Asians make up 4.5 percent of Australia's 18 million population and around one-third of the 100,000 immigrants who arrive every year.

"We must strive for a society where respect for racial equality is so deep-seated that occasional irresponsible outbursts, whether in parliament or elsewhere, go nowhere because no-one is listening," Wilson said.
Wilson said it was "a time to reflect critically" on Australia's performance on human rights.
"It is a time to consider our values as a nation," he said.

He cited as a positive step a bipartisan resolution in the Australian parliament in October supporting equal rights reagardless of race, colour, creed or origin, racial tolerance and cultural diversity.

The resolution was passed in an attempt to quell the race debate, which still lingers. But grass-roots opposition to racism is growing, with some 25,000 people attending an anti-racism march in Melbourne on Sunday.
On the negative side of the human rights ledger, Wilson said two of Australia's six states, Tasmania and Western Australia, had no protection against discrimination on the grounds of sex.
Tasmania's anti-homosexual laws, which carry a maximum jail term of 25 years for men who have sexual intercourse with each other, have been criticised by the United Nations.

Wilson said Australia needed to improve its treatment of asylum-seekers. Some Asian asylum-seekers have been held in detention camps for more than a year pending a government decision on their applications.
He also cited the continuing plight of Aborigines in Australia as a blight on the nation's human rights record.
Australia's 300,000 Aborigines are the most disadvantaged group in society, with an adult life expectancy 10 to 15 years less than non-indigenous Australians.
"It is sobering for me to reflect that if I had been born aboriginal, I would have been dead for 20 years," said Wilson, who is in his early seventies.
Wilson warned that Australia would be judged in 1997 on its response to his report on the separation of aboriginal children from their parents under a now-defunct government policy.

Tens of thousands of pale-skinned aboriginal children, called "The Stolen Generation" by Aborigines, were forcibly removed from their parents and raised in missions under a government assimilation policy until the mid-1960s.
Wilson has in the past called for an official apology from the government as a means of reconciliation between black and white Australia -- a move opposed by Prime Minister John Howard.
"The law and mechanisms (to protect human rights) are practically all in place, but justice must still be done and be seen to be done," Wilson said.
"We must recommit ourselves to the promotion of human rights and responsibilities in all their manifestations," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373 1800
